prompt: Human: Can you explain how GPS works?
response:
GPS stands for Global Positioning System.

When an object is launched into space or sends out signals about itself, the radio signals bounce back to an antenna located in a nearby ground station. If an object hasn't transmitted information or is too far away to send radio signals back, the station will know that something is nearby.

The station listens out for these radio signals. One or multiple signals are sent back by objects in nearby orbit. If the station receives the signal, it tells a network of satellites where it is and also where it was previously. This has a lot of practical uses, like tracking satellites or detecting land masses. 

In a broader sense, GPS has made many aspects of modern life easier and more efficient, like navigation, monitoring, and communication.

prompt: Human: I have a general question. I was wondering if baking powder and baking soda the same thing?
response:
Yes, baking powder and baking soda are often used interchangeably, but they actually serve different purposes. 

Baking soda, which is also known as sodium bicarbonate, is an ingredient that is naturally derived. When mixed with water, it gives off carbon dioxide and turns the mixture into a gel-like dough.  This produces a lighter, crisper texture in baked goods, much like the bubbles of gas produced by expanding air, but without the bubbles in its presence. In comparison, baking powder, which is often made of a mixture of cornstarch and chemicals, produces a less light mixture and creates that same gelling effect.

However, it's important to remember that baking soda is often substituted for baking powder in recipes when there are no specific instructions to use baking powder specifically.  That being said, it can also be used interchangeably when the recipe calls for the lighter mixture of flour and water rather than using baking powder which typically contains both flour and chemicals.

prompt: Human: What can I do to become a faster reader?

Reading speed is usually measured in pages per minute, which, according to the Reading Research Society of America, is at least 300 words per minute, or about 25 words per minute of every sentence.

One way to slow down reading is to increase your visual attention. What I mean by "visual attention" is that you're intentionally paying more attention to the text as it moves toward your eye. But it doesn't mean that you just stop looking out the window while reading. You can concentrate your attention on the text at the same time. For example, you might look up into the sky to notice the changes of the sun, the wind and clouds. Or you might study the pictures and notice them as well. 

Another important thing is to read as if you are saying what you've just read aloud. The way you read has a significant impact on how fast you can read. Reading aloud often requires you to concentrate on your word, because you're paying particular attention to the words as they move on the page. But if you try to read as if you're saying what you've just read aloud, you'll start to read in shorter sentences.

Reading fast doesn't mean reading "word for word" or as fast as you can. You can study a text very fast by skipping over certain sections of text. You can choose to take time to read each sentence separately. That's called skimming, just like when you skim an article for headlines. Another option is to read the article slowly and then skip over parts that aren't important to your understanding. You might go back to the first sentence, or the last, skipping over other sentences of the same paragraph.  
  
The above tips to speed reading all depend on you reading "word for word", meaning you must memorize whole sentences, paragraphs, and even paragraphs. That will not improve your reading speed in the long run.

Turkey is traditionally roasted and served with gravy. Here is a basic recipe for turkey. You can adapt it to any desired level of fluffiness. It will run like 15 minutes and up to 45 minutes to cook depending on the turkey.

Ingredients:
8 (or more) pounds (1 ½ kg) turkey breast (1) cut into 1 inch (25 mm) cubes; (2) 1 (½) cup (75 grams) all-purpose, unsalted flour or cornmeal
1/2 cup (120 ml (2 fluid ounces)) vegetable oil (or canola or ground olive oil) for frying
2 eggs, beaten
Salt and freshly ground pepper

1/2 teaspoon dried thyme, or 2 teaspoons fresh thyme, finely chopped
1/2 cup (10 grams) unsalted butter, room temperature
2 tablespoons all-purpose flour
2 tablespoons chopped fresh parsley
1 tablespoon olive oil or vegetable oil
1 large carrot, diced (or 2 to 3 stalks, thinly sliced)
1 medium onion, finely chopped
1 (28-ounce, 790-gram) can condensed cream of chicken soup, or the equivalent number of cans of chicken, drained, packed with their juice, or (for Turkey Day) turkey soup, as needed (about 5 large cups)
1/2 onion, diced (or 2 stalks, very thinly sliced)
1 tablespoon whole mustard seeds (for a spice rub)
1 tablespoon tomato paste
2 tablespoons hot water or stock
1/2 teaspoon ground nutmeg
1/4 teaspoon ground clove
1 teaspoon ground allspice
1 teaspoon ground white pepper
1 teaspoon ground cinnamon
A pinch of salt and freshly ground pepper
In a wide bottom baking pan with a rack (so it's ready to drain the fat), pound or shape the turkey into a 5 1/2-inch-by-8-inch (1.4-centimeter-by-20-cm) cross section.
Sprinkle all-purpose flour over the turkey, and rub it in lightly with your fingers or with a clean, well-floured knife. Do this 3 or 4 times. If you really don't like having bits of the dry, white chickenflour on your hands after you use the flour as a seasoning, you can put the flour in a fine sieve, add a bit of water at a time, and pour it over the turkey while it's still hot, shaking the pan to get as much flour into the turkey as possible. The flour mixture will get "dried" and then turn between your fingers into a fine flour-like powder, then spread all over the turkey (so make sure you get as much of the flour in for the turkey itself as possible, and that you can mix the flour with the meat so it blends in well). This is only for seasoning, to add flavor to the turkey, not strictly to make it fluffier. You can also use cornmeal or bread crumbs. Whatever you use, make sure it is a small amount. Sprinkle the turkey with salt and pepper and pepper them lightly, and then let the turkey sit for about 5 minutes, to allow the salt and pepper to get evenly distributed and absorbed. Heat a 1 to 1/2-inch (1/4-inch) vegetable oil in a deep skillet or a deep Dutch oven to about 350-375˚F (180-190˚C), and then add the turkey pieces to the hot oil, and cook, turning them once, for about 5 minutes (or until the thickest part of the meat can be felt, but not brown). Remove the turkey from the skillet and allow to drain the oil on paper towels or colander.
Put the turkey pieces through a fine mesh sieve, so they get as many of their excess oil into the sieve as possible, so they don't get too oily. Also put the turkey pieces to the side so that they are not swimming in the pan. Preheat the sauté pan over medium-high heat. Add the butter, and when it has melted (and you are sure it will not burn) add the vegetable oil. Once it has come up to temperature, and there are some splatters of oil left over on the top of the oil, add the onion and carrot, and cook, stirring occasionally, for about 20 minutes, or until just beginning to get a light-caramelized color. Season with salt and pepper, and add the flour to the pan to help the onions cook, about 5 minutes. Remove the sauté pan from the heat and stir in the cream of chicken soup, then add some of it and stir some more to get it all combined, then stir in the thyme, mustard and tomato the soup. It will have thicken up by now and become smooth and liquid. Add the beef broth and bring to a boil. When it's very hot, stir in the nutmeg, ginger, cinnamon, clove, allspice and pepper. Do that for about 1 minute until spicy aromatics and all seasoning work together. Keep an eye on it, to prevent burn, and then add salt and pepper to taste. Finally stir in the flour mixture, and then remove it all. Stir in your parsley, butter pieces, your onions, carrots, and the turkey pieces and return the pan to the heat to melt the butter, mix everything all together, and allow to cook for about 15 minutes or until the turkey browns, and the sauce thickens and coats the inside well. Pour your turkey gravy in the pan, to help the liquid in mix with the turkey. At this point is is ok to remove your turkey and serve it with gravy, either warmed from the pan or poured over fresh dinner rolls. And enjoy yourself and your turkey!
